original_interpretation: SIA reported global semiconductor sales of $791.7 billion in 2025, up 25.6% from a revised $630.5 billion in 2024, with logic up 39.9% to $301.9 billion and memory up 34.8% to $223.1 billion.
evidence_found: "global semiconductor sales hit $791.7 billion in 2025, an increase of 25.6% compared to the 2024 total of $630.5 billion"; "Sales of logic products increased by 39.9%, totaling $301.9 billion"; "Memory products ... increasing by 34.8% in 2024 [sic] to a total of $223.1 billion" (SIA release, 6 Feb 2026). WSTS 6 Mar 2026: "Global semiconductor sales reached USD 795.6 billion in 2025, representing an increase of 26.2 percent".
correction: WSTS final 2025 results (6 Mar 2026): US$795.6bn, +26.2%. WSTS Spring 2026 table: logic US$299.5bn (+38.8%), memory US$230.0bn (+39.0%). Use these instead of SIA's preliminary US$791.7bn / US$301.9bn / US$223.1bn. See the new superseding claim.
notes: SIA's February figures are preliminary (3-month moving averages). They match the page exactly; the page itself mistypes the memory year as 2024. The headline and segment values were then revised by WSTS's finalised full-year data.

original_interpretation: SIA's February 2026 release gives 2024 global semiconductor sales as $630.5 billion (revised).
evidence_found: "global semiconductor sales hit $791.7 billion in 2025, an increase of 25.6% compared to the 2024 total of $630.5 billion" (SIA, 6 Feb 2026). Feb 2025 SIA page: "Updated March 3, 2025: ... WSTS updated 2024 year-end sales to a total of $630.5 billion." WSTS Autumn 2025 table: 2024 "Total World - $M 630,549".
notes: The Feb 2026 release does not itself use the word 'revised'; the revision is documented on the Feb 2025 release page. WSTS's final 2025 figure (795.6bn, +26.2%) implies a 2024 base of about 630.5bn, so it is unchanged.

original_interpretation: High Performance Computing (which includes AI/data-center chips) rose from 51% of TSMC net revenue in 2024 to 58% in 2025, versus 29% for smartphones in 2025.
evidence_found: Net Revenue by Platform table, columns 2025 / 2024: "High Performance Computing 58% 51%"; "Smartphone 29% 35%" (TSMC 4Q25 Management Report, 15 Jan 2026, p. 1).
notes: Company-reported, unaudited management report; full-year 2025 is the latest complete year as of 2026-10-01. Saying HPC 'includes AI/data-center chips' is the researcher's gloss; the report does not define HPC.

original_interpretation: TSMC's 2025 net revenue was NT$3,809.05 billion (up 31.6%), or US$122.42 billion (up 35.9%).
evidence_found: "Full Year 2025 ... Net revenue was NT$3,809.05 billion, representing a 31.6% increase from 2024. In US dollar terms, net revenue increased 35.9% to US$122.42 billion in 2025." Summary table: Net Revenue (US$ billions) 2025 122.42 vs 2024 90.08 (TSMC 4Q25 Management Report, p. 1).
notes: Checked the arithmetic: 3,809.05/2,894.31 = +31.6% and 122.42/90.08 = +35.9%. These are company management-report figures, consistent with what TSMC reports in its filings.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG (2021) reported that 100% of the world's below-10nm (leading-edge) logic capacity was in Taiwan (92%) and South Korea (8%), a figure the USITC attributes to 2019.
evidence_found: "100% of the world's most advanced (below 10 nanometers) semiconductor manufacturing capacity is currently located in Taiwan (92%) and South Korea (8%)." (SIA-BCG 2-pager, 2021). USITC WP 2023-11-A: "in 2019, Taiwan dominated the advanced logic chip manufacturing—technology node under 10nm—with a 92 percent of fabrication capacity, while South Korea accounted for the remaining 8 percent".
notes: This is a dated (2019) BCG estimate, correctly labelled. Newer data: the SIA/BCG May 2024 summary says US advanced-logic (<10nm) capacity was 0% in 2022, and BCG describes 2022 capacity as 'almost 100%' in Taiwan and South Korea. The 2022 Taiwan/Korea split is shown only in a chart and was not verified here. The USITC PDF is blocked in the browser (403) but readable via web_extract.

original_interpretation: SIA/BCG (2021) estimated about 75% of global semiconductor manufacturing capacity was in China and East Asia, and identified more than 50 points in the value chain where one region held over 65% of global share.
evidence_found: "There are more than 50 points across the value chain where one region holds more than 65% of the global market share." "About 75% of global semiconductor manufacturing capacity, for example, is concentrated in China and East Asia" (SIA-BCG 2-pager, March 2021, p. 2).
notes: Verbatim wording found (the researcher had recorded it as a paraphrase). This is a BCG estimate for about 2020, so claim_type estimate is correct.

original_interpretation: In December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs achieved transistor action in a germanium point-contact device (historical, 1947).
evidence_found: "JOHN BARDEEN & WALTER BRATTAIN ACHIEVE TRANSISTOR ACTION IN A GERMANIUM POINT-CONTACT DEVICE IN DECEMBER 1947."; "On December 16, 1947, their research culminated in the first successful semiconductor amplifier." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1947 milestone).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier. web_extract returned 404 for the no-trailing-slash URL; the browser opened the cited URL.

original_interpretation: Robert Noyce (Fairchild) filed his monolithic integrated circuit patent in July 1959, and Fairchild engineers produced the first working monolithic ICs by May 1960 (historical).
evidence_found: "Noyce filed his \"Semiconductor device-and-lead structure\" patent in July 1959 and a team of Fairchild engineers produced the first working monolithic ICs in May 1960." Contemporary documents: U.S. Patent 2981877 "(Filed July 30, 1959. Issued April 25, 1961)" (CHM Silicon Engine, 1959 milestone).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: In April 1952, over 100 representatives from 40 companies that had paid a $25,000 patent-licensing fee attended Bell Labs' Transistor Technology Symposium, spreading transistor know-how to firms including GE, RCA, Texas Instruments and Sony (historical, 1952).
evidence_found: "In April 1952, over 100 representatives from 40 companies that had paid a $25,000 patent-licensing fee came for a nine-day Transistor Technology Symposium"; "There were participants from such electronics titans as GE and RCA, as well as from then-small firms like Texas Instruments and Sony." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1952 milestone).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: In 1971 Intel's 4004, a 4-bit CPU on a single chip with about 2,300 transistors, was implemented by Federico Faggin and Masatoshi Shima (historical; commonly described as the first commercial microprocessor).
evidence_found: "Ted Hoff and Stanley Mazor conceived Intel's first integrated CPU, the 4004 4-bit device ... In 1971, Federico Faggin, assisted by Masatoshi Shima, applied his experience in silicon-gate MOS technology ... to squeeze the 2300 transistors of the 4004 into a low-cost 16-pin package." The page also describes earlier CPU chips: Four-Phase AL-1 (1969) and Garrett AiResearch MP944 (1970).
correction: The source supports 1971, 4-bit, about 2,300 transistors, and implementation by Faggin assisted by Shima (conceived by Hoff and Mazor). It does not call the 4004 'the first commercial microprocessor', and it lists earlier CPU-on-chip efforts (Four-Phase AL-1, MP944). That parenthetical is unsupported by this source.
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: Gordon Moore's article 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' was published in Electronics on April 19, 1965, projecting a doubling of components per chip every 12 months; in 1975 he revised the rate to a doubling every two years (historical).
evidence_found: "Extrapolating the trend to 1975 he projected that the number of components per chip would reach 65,000; a doubling every 12 months. ... \"Cramming more components onto integrated circuits\" was published in Electronics on April 19, 1965."; in 1975 "he slowed the future rate of increase in complexity to \"a doubling every two years, rather than every year.\"" (CHM, 1965 milestone).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: Beginning in 1970, Intel's 1103 MOS DRAM, priced at 1 cent per bit, quickly replaced magnetic core memory for computer main memory (historical).
evidence_found: "Offering much faster speed and priced at 1 cent/bit, beginning in 1970 the 1103 quickly replaced magnetic core technology for computer main memory." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1970 milestone).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: Jean Hoerni at Fairchild wrote a patent disclosure for the planar process in January 1959 and demonstrated a working planar transistor in March 1959; planar devices allowed all components of an integrated circuit to be fabricated from one side of a wafer (historical, 1959).
evidence_found: "After writing a patent disclosure in January 1959, he demonstrated a working planar transistor that March."; "And they permitted fabrication of all the components of an integrated circuit from one side of a wafer (1960 Milestone)." (CHM Silicon Engine, 1959 planar milestone).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: On September 12, 1958 Jack Kilby successfully tested the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments (historical, 1958).
evidence_found: "September 12, 1958 Successful Test of the First Integrated Circuit. Jack Kilby successfully tests the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments to prove that resistors and capacitors could exist on the same piece of semiconductor material." (CHM This Day in History, Sept 12).
notes: CHM is a museum (source_type 'other', tier 3); primary documents (patents, journal papers) are listed on the page but were not opened, so confidence stays capped by tier.

original_interpretation: According to the Computer History Museum, Lynn Conway's work (co-author of the Mead-Conway text 'Introduction to VLSI Systems') and rapid chip-prototyping infrastructure, institutionalised through DARPA's MOSIS, spawned the 'fabless-design + silicon-foundry' paradigm in the 1980s.
evidence_found: Conway "became principal author of the famous Mead-Conway text Introduction to VLSI systems"; "invented and demonstrated an internet e-commerce infrastructure for rapid chip prototyping, spawning the \"fabless-design + silicon-foundry\" paradigm ... Institutionalized by DARPA at USC-ISI, the resulting \"MOSIS\" system enabled ... thousands of chip designs, leading to many major startups in the 80's" (CHM Fellow profile).
notes: The claim correctly attributes this to the museum. It is a laudatory Fellow-profile characterisation rather than an established fact, so 'reported_claim' or an attributed interpretation would fit better than 'fact'. CHM credits the prototyping infrastructure (not the textbook) with spawning the paradigm.

original_interpretation: Jack Kilby received half of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit'.
evidence_found: "The Nobel Prize in Physics 2000 was awarded ... with one half jointly to Zhores I. Alferov and Herbert Kroemer ... and the other half to Jack S. Kilby \"for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit\"" (NobelPrize.org, Physics 2000 summary).
notes: nobelprize.org is the prize-awarder's official record. Classifying it as source_type 'other' (tier 3) understates it, but the claim is fully supported.

original_interpretation: TSMC was established in 1987 by Morris Chang and describes itself as having pioneered the pure-play foundry business model, manufacturing only its customers' products.
evidence_found: "Established in 1987 by Dr. Morris Chang, TSMC (TWSE: 2330, NYSE: TSM) pioneered the pure-play foundry business model with an exclusive focus on manufacturing its customers' products." (About TSMC). ITRI: "ITRI set up the spin-off company Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) which introduced the world's first IC OEM operation model."
notes: Correctly typed as reported_claim (company self-description), so confidence is capped at medium. ITRI's account independently supports the 'first' foundry model.

original_interpretation: UMC switched from an integrated device manufacturer (IDM) model to a pure-play foundry model in 1995.
evidence_found: UMC Overview, 'A Long and Productive History': "1995 Switched from IDM to pure-play foundry model".
notes: Company milestone list (reported_claim, correctly typed).

original_interpretation: ITRI, Taiwan's state-founded research institute, set up UMC in 1980 as a spin-off, transferring 4-inch wafer technology and its R&D team; UMC was Taiwan's first IC company.
evidence_found: "ITRI set up United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) in 1980 and transferred the 4-inch wafer technology along with its R&D team to this spin-off company. UMC was Taiwan's first IC company" (ITRI 50th history page). UMC: "1980 Spun off from state-owned ITRI as Taiwan's first IC company".
notes: Both parties to the spin-off agree. The ITRI 50th-anniversary page is an institutional history (source_type 'other'); ITRI is a government-founded institute.

original_interpretation: Morris Chang was invited by Taiwan's Premier Yun-Suan Sun to return to Taiwan in 1985 to serve as President of ITRI, before ITRI spun off TSMC in 1987.
evidence_found: "Dr. Morris Chang was invited by Premier Yun-Suan Sun to return to Taiwan in 1985 and serve as the President of ITRI to govern the development of the 6-inch wafer technology."; "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) was established the next year [1987]. ITRI transferred fabs, equipment, technology, and 98 professionals to TSMC" (ITRI 50th history page).

original_interpretation: A US Commerce Department RFI (published January 2022) found that median inventory of semiconductor products held by buyers fell from 40 days in 2019 to less than 5 days in 2021.
evidence_found: "The median inventory of semiconductor products highlighted by buyers has fallen from 40 days in 2019 to less than 5 days in 2021 (see Figure 2)." Later: "For the semiconductor products that present the greatest challenge to acquire, the median inventory for consumers who responded to the RFI has fallen from 40 days in 2019 to less than 5 days" (Commerce blog, 25 Jan 2022).
notes: Wording caveat: the RFI was launched in September 2021 (more than 150 responses, due November); January 2022 is when the results were published. The population is only the hardest-to-acquire products highlighted by respondent buyers, not all chip inventory. The commerce.gov browser view is Cloudflare-gated; web_extract returned the full text.

original_interpretation: The Commerce RFI found semiconductor fabs operated at over 90% utilization from Q2 2020 through 2021 and identified wafer production capacity as the primary bottleneck.
evidence_found: "Specifically, from Q2 of 2020 through 2021, semiconductor fabs operated at over 90% utilization" (Figure 1 source: SIA 2021 State of the U.S. Semiconductor Industry); "The primary bottleneck across the board appears to be wafer production capacity, which requires a longer-term solution." (Commerce, 25 Jan 2022).
notes: The utilization figure is Commerce citing SIA's 2021 report, not RFI data. The claim's phrase 'The Commerce RFI found ... utilization' slightly misattributes it. The bottleneck finding is from the RFI.

original_interpretation: Median chip demand highlighted by buyers in the Commerce RFI was as much as 17% higher in 2021 than in 2019.
evidence_found: "Median demand for chips highlighted by buyers was as much as 17% higher in 2021 than 2019, and buyers aren't seeing commensurate increases in the supply they receive." (Commerce, 25 Jan 2022, key findings).

original_interpretation: On April 17, 1987 President Reagan, invoking Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, imposed 100% ad valorem duties on about $300 million of Japanese exports for Japan's failure to meet the 1986 Semiconductor Arrangement's market-access and anti-dumping commitments.
evidence_found: Memo of April 17, 1987: "to proclaim increases in customs duties to a level of 100 percent ad valorem on certain products of Japan ... effective with respect to the covered products of Japan which are entered on and after April 17, 1987"; "On March 27, 1987, I announced my intention to raise customs duties to a level of 100 percent ad valorem on as much as $300 million in Japanese exports".
correction: The US$300 million is a ceiling announced on 27 March 1987 ('as much as $300 million'), not a stated covered value. The 17 April memo proclaims 100% duties on 'certain products of Japan' and does not give the trade value covered. The Section 301 basis and the market-access and anti-dumping failures are supported.

original_interpretation: The United States and Japan formally signed the Semiconductor Arrangement on September 2, 1986, under which Japan agreed to facilitate market access for foreign chipmakers in Japan and to prevent dumping of semiconductors in the US and in third-country markets.
evidence_found: "On September 2, 1986, the United States and Japan formally signed the Arrangement ... The Japanese government agreed to [-] facilitate increased market access opportunities for foreign semiconductor firms in Japan, [-] prevent the dumping of semiconductors in the United States, and [-] prevent the dumping of semiconductors in third country markets." (GAO/NSIAD-87-134BR, p. 3).
notes: web_extract returned only fragments of this scanned PDF. Downloaded it via the browser and extracted the text with pypdf to read the passage.

original_interpretation: US semiconductor and computer companies formed the SEMATECH consortium in August 1987, with anticipated federal funding of $100 million per year and an initial mission to help the US industry regain world manufacturing leadership by the end of 1992.
evidence_found: "several U.S. semiconductor and computer companies formed SEMATECH in August 1987"; "It was anticipated that the federal government would provide $100 million per year to SEMATECH over a 5-year period through fiscal year 1992" (p. 1-2); "SEMATECH'S initial mission was to enable the U.S. semiconductor industry to regain world leadership in manufacturing by the end of 1992." (p. 4) (GAO/RCED-92-283).
notes: The page numbers are the report's printed page numbers (PDF pp. 3-6). The funding was anticipated over five years through FY1992. Members provided at least half of SEMATECH's roughly US$200m annual budget.

original_interpretation: Market share evidence on the 1990-2020 shift: according to SIA's summary of a 2020 BCG study, the US share of global semiconductor manufacturing capacity fell from 37% in 1990 to 12% (circa 2020).
evidence_found: "U.S. companies account for 48% of the world's chip sales, but U.S.-located fabs only account for 12% of the world's semiconductor manufacturing, down from 37% in 1990." (SIA Summary of BCG report, Sept 2020). SIA 2024 summary: "decreasing from 37% in 1990 to 12% in 2020, and further declining to 10% as of 2022".
notes: The c.2020 figure is accurate and is reconfirmed by SIA/BCG (May 2024). Newer data: 10% as of 2022, projected 14% by 2032 (200mm+ commercial fab capacity), already recorded as CLM-0563. This is a time series, so the c.2020 value is not superseded.

original_interpretation: SIA's summary of the 2020 BCG study attributed 40-70% of the 30-50% total-cost-of-ownership gap between US fabs and fabs in competing Asian locations to government incentives.
evidence_found: "Depending on the type of fab, a new fab in the U.S. costs approximately 30% more to build and operate over 10 years than one in Taiwan, South Korea, or Singapore, and 37-50% more than one in China. As much as 40-70% of that cost differential is directly attributed to government incentives." (SIA Summary of BCG report, Sept 2020, Key Finding 2).
correction: The source gives an upper bound: 'as much as' 40-70% of the gap. The gap is about 30% versus Taiwan, Korea and Singapore, and 37-50% versus China, over 10 years. It is not a uniform '30-50%' gap.

original_interpretation: The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 gave the US Commerce Department $50 billion, of which $39 billion is for manufacturing incentives (CHIPS Program Office) and $11 billion for R&D.
evidence_found: "When the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 was signed into law, it provided the Department of Commerce with $50 billion ... The CHIPS Research and Development Office is investing $11 billion into developing a robust domestic R&D ecosystem, while the CHIPS Program Office is dedicating $39 billion to provide incentives for investment in facilities and equipment" (NIST, CHIPS for America).
notes: The page was still live on 2026-10-01 with this wording. These are statutory appropriation figures as described by the implementing agency, so they are historical and not superseded.

original_interpretation: On October 7, 2022 BIS imposed export controls on advanced computing chips, supercomputer end uses and semiconductor manufacturing equipment destined for the PRC, and restricted US persons from supporting certain PRC fabs without a licence.
evidence_found: "the rule imposes restrictive export controls on certain advanced computing semiconductor chips, transactions for supercomputer end-uses"; "Adds certain semiconductor manufacturing equipment and related items to the CCL"; "7.) Restricts the ability of U.S. persons to support the development, or production, of ICs at certain PRC-located semiconductor fabrication \"facilities\" without a license" (BIS release, 7 Oct 2022).
notes: 7 Oct 2022 is the date the rule was announced and filed. It took effect in phases: SME items on 7 Oct, US-person restrictions on 12 Oct, and advanced computing/supercomputer controls on 21 Oct 2022. Later rules (Oct 2023, Dec 2024, 2025) amended it. This claim is historical.

original_interpretation: On May 15, 2019 the US Commerce Department added Huawei Technologies and affiliates to the Entity List, requiring a BIS licence for the sale or transfer of US technology to them.
evidence_found: Release dated 15 May 2019: BIS "announced that it will be adding Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and its affiliates to the Bureau's Entity List"; "The listing will be effective when published in the Federal Register." 84 FR 22961 (21 May 2019): "DATES: Effective Date: This rule is effective May 16, 2019."
correction: On 15 May 2019 Commerce announced it would add Huawei and its affiliates. The listing took effect on 16 May 2019 (rule published 21 May 2019 at 84 FR 22961; 68 non-US affiliates; licence required for all items subject to the EAR, presumption of denial). See CLM-0820 and CLM-0821.
notes: The browser was blocked by Cloudflare on 2017-2021.commerce.gov; web_extract returned the press-release text.

original_interpretation: The European Chips Act entered into force on 21 September 2023, expected to mobilise more than EUR 43 billion of public investment, with an aim to double the EU's global market share from about 10% to 20% by 2030.
evidence_found: "The Chips Act entered into force on 21 September 2023." "The Chips Act should result in public investments of more than €43 billion." "the EU has only roughly 10% of global market share"; "doubling our global market share to 20% in 2030" (European Commission Chips Act factpage, read in browser).
notes: The €43bn is a Commission expectation ('should result in'), so it is an estimate within a 'fact' claim. The page also says '20% ... of cutting-edge semiconductors'. Context: EPRS (May 2026) reports that the Court of Auditors judged the 20% target unlikely, with the Commission's own forecast at 11.7% by 2030. A Chips Act 2.0 was proposed on 3 June 2026. See the new claim.

original_interpretation: SIA initially reported global semiconductor sales of $627.6 billion for 2024 (up 19.1%), with memory up 78.9% to $165.1 billion and DRAM up 82.6%.
evidence_found: "global semiconductor sales hit $627.6 billion in 2024, an increase of 19.1% compared to the 2023 total of $526.8 billion"; "Memory products were second in terms of sales, increasing by 78.9% in 2024 to a total of $165.1 billion. DRAM products, a subset of memory, recorded an 82.6% sales increase" (SIA, 7 Feb 2025). Page note: updated 3 Mar 2025 to $630.5bn.
notes: The claim is explicitly framed as the initial report, so the later revision to US$630.5bn (CLM-0127) does not make it outdated. The page shows the release date as 7 Feb 2025.
